newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOV'T SUBSIDISES FIRMS' POST-FLOOD LOANS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOV'T SUBSIDISES FIRMS' POST-FLOOD LOANS.

text.p: The Czech government approved one billion crowns of additional funds from the state budget for subsidising low-interest reconstruction loans for firms damaged in July floods, Industry and Trade Minister Karel Kuhnl said on Friday.

He told reporters that the funds would be administered through the state-controlled develoment bank Ceskomoravska Zarucni a Rozvojova Banka and were intended to subisidise interest rates on credits totalling 15 to 18 billion crowns.
Kuhnl said that the programme to subisise loans was necessary because of the current level of Czech commercial interest rates, which are hovering well above 15 percent.
"We would like to see the interest rates to be reduced but it of course depends on the fiscal and monetary situation in the Czech Republic," the minister said.
"The main reason why we started this (reconstruction) programme was exactly the high level of interest rates."
Kuhnl did not say what interest rates would be attained by businesses drawing money on the subsidies programme.

Crops, businesses, homes, and infrastructure were destroyed in the floods, the worst on record for the area which devastated large parts of the east of the country last month after torrential rains and killed over 100 people in the Czech Republic and Poland.
Total Czech damage has been estimated by the government at 60 billion crowns.

The Czech government on Wednesday approved 1.9 billion crowns from the state budget to help pay for communication and ecological problems caused by the flooding and is to request some 2.3 billion crowns in aid from the European Union through its PHARE programme.
It had already approved the issuance of five billion crowns in flood-relief bonds, and assigned around five billion crowns out of privatisation proceeds to the afflicted areas.
It is also considering a loan of more than 10 billion crowns from the European Investment Bank.
Still, ministers have said a special flood relief tax might be considered to help cover costs of the reconstruction.
